content: In mathematics, the concept of convergence of measures is studied within measure theory, and there are two primary types of convergence: strong convergence and weak convergence. Strong Convergence of Measures Consider a measurable space denoted as ((X, mathcal{F})). If the set of all measures (or, more commonly, probability measures) on ((X, mathcal{F})) can be equipped with a metric, then convergence in this metric is referred to as strong convergence. Examples of such metrics include the Radon metric and the total variation metric. Weak Convergence of Measures Weak convergence, also known as narrow convergence, is another type of convergence related to measures. There are at least five definitions of weak convergence for a sequence of measures, some of which are more general than others. The equivalence of four of these definitions for probability measures on a general topological space, along with a fifth condition specific to distributions on the real line, is often referred to as the portmanteau theorem. Let ((Omega, T)) be a topological space with its Borel (sigma)-algebra, denoted as (text{Borel}(Omega)). Let (P(Omega)) represent the collection of all probability measures defined on ((Omega, text{Borel}(Omega))). Assume (T) is separable, which implies that (P(Omega)) is metrizable. Let ((mu_n)) be a sequence in (P(Omega)), and let (mu in P(Omega)). The following conditions are equivalent: 1. For all bounded and continuous functions (f : Omega to mathbb{R}) (often called test functions), [ lim_{n to infty} int_{Omega} f , mathrm{d}mu_n = int_{Omega} f , mathrm{d}mu. ] 2. For all closed subsets (C subseteq Omega), [ limsup_{n to infty} mu_n(C) leq mu(C). ] 3. For all open subsets (U subseteq Omega), [ liminf_{n to infty} mu_n(U) geq mu(U). ] 4. For all subsets (A subseteq Omega) that are (mu)-continuity sets (i.e., sets (A) for which (mu(partial A) = 0), where (partial A) denotes the boundary of (A)), [ lim_{n to infty} mu_n(A) = mu(A). ] 5. In the specific case where (Omega = mathbb{R}) with its usual topology, if (F_n) and (F) denote the cumulative distribution functions of the measures (mu_n) and (mu), respectively, then [ lim_{n to infty} F_n(x) = F(x) quad text{for all points } x in mathbb{R} text{ at which } F text{ is continuous.} ] Definition and Notation If any (and hence all) of the above conditions hold, the sequence of measures ((mu_n)_{n=1}^infty) is said to converge weakly to (mu). Weak convergence is also referred to as narrow convergence, convergence in distribution, or convergence in law. The terms convergence in distribution and convergence in law are more commonly used when discussing the weak convergence of random variables, as described in the next section. Weak Convergence of Random Variables Let ((Omega, mathcal{F}, mathbb{P})) be a probability space, and let (X_n, X : Omega to mathbb{X}) be random variables. The sequence (X_n) is said to converge weakly (or in distribution, or in law) to (X) as (n to infty) if the sequence of pushforward measures ((X_n)_(mathbb{P})) converges weakly to (X_(mathbb{P})) in the sense of weak convergence of measures on (mathbb{X}), as defined above.
